1.goal: To open on how she feels about explaining problems at work, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
1.interaction: T–S, spoken. One open question; Portuguese is fine at this point.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class, and whether she wrote notes about a problem at work.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she explains a problem to Paula and connects the ideas.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you explain a problem at work. We work on the words that connect your ideas.”
1.expected: A short answer that names one of the two, for example “Putting the ideas together. I have the words, but the sentences are short.” Any answer is useful: it tells you what she notices about her own speaking.
1.support: If she does not understand the question, point at the two options on screen and let her choose one.
1.challenge: Ask for one example of a sentence she wanted to say last week and could not.
1.monitoring: What she says about her own difficulty.
1.transition: Move on when she has answered.

2.goal: To hear how she explains a problem before any model or rule, and to write down her sentences exactly as she says them.
2.interaction: T–S. She talks; you listen and write.
run: Read the question and the three prompts on screen with her.
Let her talk. Leave corrections and help with connecting words for later: this is the diagnostic of the lesson.
Write down her sentences word for word, especially the places where two ideas meet.
If she stops after one sentence, ask the next prompt on screen.
exact: If she stops: “And why was it a problem?”
Closing: “Thank you. I wrote down what you said. We come back to it later.”
2.expected: There is no answer key: this is her own problem. What you are listening for is how the ideas are joined. A complete explanation at this level has three parts — what happened, why, and what she did — for example “The report was late. The system was not working. We sent it the next day.” Short separate sentences, “and” for everything, or “because” with a noun are all useful evidence. The sentences you write here come back on screens 6 and 11.
2.support: If she cannot think of a problem, offer two: something that arrived late, or something that did not work.
2.challenge: Ask what happened after the problem was solved.
2.monitoring: Which connecting words she uses (because, so, but, when, and), and where she makes two sentences instead of one.
2.evidence: Her sentences, word for word, and the connecting words she used or did not use. It is the diagnostic record of the lesson.
2.transition: Move on when she has told the three parts, or has stopped after trying.

3.goal: To read a short message where the ideas are connected, first for the meaning.
run: Give her about two minutes to read the message.
Ask the question on screen.
Leave the bold words for the next screen.
exact: Before she reads: “Read it once. Find what went well, and what is still a problem.”
3.expected: What went well: the laptops arrived, Nora installed the system and fixed two laptops, and the sales team can start using the system this afternoon. What is still a problem: one laptop is still not working. A complete answer: “Nineteen laptops are working. One is still not working.”
3.support: If a word stops her, give the meaning and let her continue. Fixed and still not working were in the pre-class.
3.challenge: Ask what Ryan is going to do next, and when.
3.monitoring: Whether she understands the message as a whole.
3.evidence: Whether she found the good news and the problem without rereading.
3.transition: Move on when she has named what went well and what is still a problem.

4.goal: To have her notice that the words in bold bring four different kinds of information, before the rule is explained.
4.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S.
run: Let her choose an answer for the six sentences and press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each one, ask her which word helped her decide.
Leave the rule for screen 6.
exact: On each sentence: “Which word tells you that?”
4.expected: The result: “The laptops arrived on Wednesday at five, so Nora started the installation that evening.” · “The sales team has nineteen laptops now, so they can start using the new system this afternoon.” The reason: “The installation took longer than we expected because two laptops had a problem with the password.” · “The meeting started late because the room was not free.” Something different: “Nora fixed them on Thursday morning, but one laptop is still not working.” The time: “I will ask the supplier for a new one when they call me today.”
4.support: On each sentence, ask: does the second part say why, what happened after, or something different?
4.challenge: Ask her to change one of the so sentences into a because sentence.
4.monitoring: Whether she separates the reason from the result. Mixing these two is the most useful thing to notice.
4.evidence: Which sentences she placed in another group.
4.transition: Move on when the six are sorted.

5.goal: To have her find what changes between a because sentence and a so sentence with the same information.
run: Read the two sentences with her.
Ask the questions on screen, and let her answer before you open the button.
Open the answer and read it with her. Ask for one pair of her own about her problem from screen 2.
exact: If she does not see it: “In the first sentence, what comes first: the problem or the result?”
Asking for her pair: “Say your problem with because. Now say it with so.”
5.expected: The facts are the same; the order changes. After because comes the reason (two laptops had a problem); after so comes the result (the installation took longer). From the reveal: result + because + reason; reason + so + result. Her own pair can be short, for example “The report was late because the system was not working. / The system was not working, so the report was late.”
5.support: Draw an arrow in the air from the reason to the result, and ask where the arrow starts in each sentence.
5.challenge: Ask which of the two sentences is better when Paula asks “Why was it late?”.
5.monitoring: Whether her own pair keeps the reason after because and the result after so.
5.transition: Move on when she has made one pair of her own.

6.goal: To clarify the meaning, the form and the sound of the five connecting words, and to go back to her sentence from screen 2.
6.interaction: T–S, with the table on screen.
run: Read the table with her, one row at a time.
On because of, ask what is different about what comes after it.
Read the box about sound, and say because in a fast sentence for her to repeat.
Ask the question on screen: read one of her sentences from screen 2, and ask which word she used or could use.
exact: CCQ for because of: “Can I say because of the laptops had a problem?” (No. Because of + a noun: because of the problem.)
CCQ for so: “In ‘They arrived at five, so Nora started’, did Nora start first?” (No. They arrived first.)
Going back to screen 2: “You said: ‘…’. Which word could join these two ideas?”
6.expected: From the table: because + subject + verb (the reason); because of + a noun (the reason); so + subject + verb (the result); but + subject + verb (something different); when + subject + verb (the time). On her sentence from screen 2, a complete answer names a word and says the new sentence, for example “The system was not working, so the report was late.”
6.support: If because of is hard, give two endings and let her choose: “because of the rain” or “because of it was raining”.
6.challenge: Ask her to join three ideas from her problem in one sentence with two different words.
6.monitoring: Whether she can answer the two CCQs, and whether her new sentence uses the form in the table.
6.evidence: Her answer to the CCQs, and her sentence from screen 2 rebuilt.
6.transition: Move on when she has rebuilt one of her sentences.

7.goal: To choose the right connecting word in five sentences, check, and say them out loud.
7.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S, spoken.
run: Let her complete the five sentences with the words in the box and press Check.
Go through the answers. On each wrong one, ask what comes after the gap: a reason, a result, something different, or a time.
Play the two model sentences. Then ask her to say all five sentences out loud.
exact: On a wrong answer: “What comes after the gap? A reason or a result?”
7.expected: “The client did not answer, so I called again.” · “We could not start the meeting because the projector was not working.” · “The flight was late because of the weather.” · “The report is ready, but the numbers from June are missing.” · “Ryan will tell the team when he gets the new laptop.” The one most often confused is because and because of: the projector was not working has a verb, and the weather is a noun.
7.support: If she hesitates between because and because of, ask: is there a verb after the gap?
7.challenge: Ask her to say sentence 1 again with because instead of so.
7.monitoring: Whether she chooses by meaning or by guessing, and whether because sounds short in her sentences.
7.evidence: Which items were wrong at first, and whether the spoken sentences keep the right word.
7.transition: Move on when the five are checked and said.

8.goal: To join pairs of facts into one sentence with the right word, about a situation she chooses.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken, one pair at a time.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose.
With option B, give her a moment to write four pairs of facts on paper.
Ask for one sentence for each pair. Let her say it; if the word does not fit, ask what comes after it.
exact: Starting option A: “Pair one. Join the two facts in one sentence.”
If the word does not fit: “What comes after so? Is that the result?”
8.expected: Option A, possible sentences: 1 — “The printer is broken, so we printed the report on the first floor.” 2 — “The client meeting moved to Friday because the client is traveling on Thursday.” 3 — “The new system is faster, but some people do not like it.” 4 — “Nora installs the system when the new laptop arrives.” Other words are correct when the meaning works, for example pair 1 with “because”: “We printed the report on the first floor because the printer is broken.” Option B has no fixed content: four sentences, each with a word that fits the relation between the facts.
8.support: Cover one fact and ask what the relation is: why, what happened after, or something different.
8.challenge: Ask her to say pair 2 in the other order, with so.
8.monitoring: Whether she chooses the word by the relation between the facts.
8.evidence: Which words she used without help, and which relation was hardest.
8.transition: Move on when the four pairs are joined.

9.goal: To explain a problem to Paula with the ideas connected: what happened, why, what she did, and what happens next.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are Paula; she explains.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose.
Give her a moment to look at the notes, or to think about her own problem.
Let her explain without interruption. The sentence starters stay closed unless she stops.
Write down one sentence as she said it, for screen 11.
exact: Opening: “Hi. Ryan said there's still a problem. What's going on?”
9.expected: Option A, a complete explanation with connected ideas: “One laptop is still not working because there is a problem with the screen. I called the supplier, but they did not answer. When they call back, I will ask for a new one.” Option B has no fixed content: the same four parts about her problem, with at least two connecting words. Compare it with her sentences from screen 2.
9.support: If she stops, point at the next line of the notes before you open the starters.
9.challenge: Ask her to add what the problem means for the sales team, with so.
9.monitoring: Which connecting words appear without looking at the screen, and whether because and so keep their order.
9.evidence: How many connecting words she used, and one sentence word for word, to compare with screen 2.
9.transition: Move on when she has explained the four parts.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after the explanation: answer why and what next, and ask one question back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still Paula.
run: Ask the two questions below, one at a time.
Wait after each answer, so she can add the reason or the result.
Then invite her to ask you one question, and answer it.
exact: Question 1, option A: “Why can't Nora fix it?” Option B: “Why did that happen?”
Question 2: “And what happens if the supplier doesn't call back today?”
Handing the turn over: “Do you need anything from me?”
10.expected: Option A: “Because it is a problem with the screen, not with the password.” and “I will call them again tomorrow morning, so we can have a new laptop this week.” Option B: answers about her own problem, each with a reason or a result. Her question can be short, for example “Can you call the supplier too?”.
10.support: If she answers with one word, ask “Why?” once more and wait.
10.challenge: Push back once: “I don't want to wait. What else can we do?”
10.monitoring: Whether her answers keep a connecting word under pressure.
10.evidence: Whether she answered with a connected idea, and whether she asked a question of her own.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To compare her sentence from screen 2 with a connected version, and to tell the problem again to a new listener.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve.
Write her sentence from screen 2 in the third box, and build the connected version with her in the fourth box.
Open the replay. You are a new colleague who does not know the team. She tells the problem again and uses the sentence from the fourth box.
exact: Opening the replay: “Hi, I'm new here. I heard something about a laptop problem. What happened?”
11.expected: The same problem, told to someone who does not know Ryan or Nora, with the sentence from the fourth box in it. A complete second version explains who the people are in a few words, for example “Ryan, our coordinator, ordered new laptops, but one is still not working because…”.
11.support: Point at the fourth box and let her read the sentence the first time.
11.challenge: Ask a “why” question in the middle, and let her answer with because.
11.monitoring: Whether the sentence from the fourth box appears, and whether other ideas are connected too.
11.evidence: The difference between her sentence from screen 2 and her sentences in the replay.
11.transition: Move on when the replay is done.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when you explain something at work, join the reason and the result in one sentence.”
12.expected: The recap has six lines: explaining a problem before any model, reading a message where the ideas are connected, because and so, the five words and what comes after them, joining two facts, and explaining a problem to Paula and answering why. The confidence scale is hers.
12.support: If she marks everything low, read her connected sentence from the fourth box.
12.challenge: Ask which of the five words she wants to use more.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson is the weekly check-in: her own update, with questions.
